content: The Advanced Emergency Medical Technician Critical Care (EMT-CC) certification is specific to New York State and represents a level of training that surpasses the national EMT-Intermediate/99 (EMT-I/99) standard. EMT-CCs are classified as Advanced Life Support (ALS) providers and are trained in advanced airway management, intravenous (IV) fluid administration, cardiac monitoring and defibrillation, as well as the administration of medications for both adult and pediatric patients. To become an EMT-CC, candidates must first hold a current EMT-Basic certification. Most training programs require at least one year of active experience at the EMT-Basic level. The training program typically involves 300 to 400 hours of instruction, divided into 175 to 225 hours of classroom and practical laboratory work, 50 to 75 hours of clinical experience, and 75 to 100 hours of field internship. At the conclusion of the program, students must pass both a state practical skills exam and a written exam to achieve certification. Continuing medical education is required to maintain certification, ensuring that EMT-CCs remain up-to-date with evolving medical practices. In the classroom, students cover a wide range of topics, including the foundations of critical care, human systems, roles and responsibilities, emergency pharmacology, venous access, medication administration, airway management, ventilation, patient assessment, history taking, physical examination techniques, clinical decision-making, communication, and documentation. Trauma-related topics include trauma systems, mechanisms of injury, hemorrhage, shock, burns, and head, thoracic, and abdominal trauma. Medical emergencies addressed include respiratory, cardiovascular, diabetic, allergic reactions, poisonings, overdoses, neurological emergencies, non-traumatic abdominal emergencies, environmental emergencies, behavioral emergencies, gynecological and obstetrical emergencies, neonatal resuscitation, pediatrics, and geriatrics. In clinical settings, students observe healthcare professionals in environments such as emergency departments, operating rooms, coronary care units, pediatric intensive care units, neonatal intensive care units, burn units, and medical intensive care units. This clinical exposure allows students to practice and refine their skills and knowledge in a supervised, educational setting. During field training, EMT-CC students participate in EMS calls requiring ALS skills under the supervision of an EMT-CC or paramedic preceptor. This phase of training focuses on applying cognitive knowledge and practical skills developed in the classroom and clinical settings to real-world EMS scenarios. EMT-CCs operate under a set of protocols for patient care, guided by a medical director. These protocols are often presented in algorithmic formats and include standing orders or orders requiring direct communication with medical control via radio or telephone. Compared to paramedics, EMT-CCs have fewer standing orders and require more frequent contact with medical control. Protocols vary slightly across New York regions but adhere to current guidelines for Advanced Cardiac Life Support (ACLS), Pediatric Advanced Life Support (PALS), Pre-hospital Trauma Life Support (PHTLS), Basic Trauma Life Support (BTLS), and Advanced Trauma Life Support (ATLS). EMT-CCs are trained to perform a variety of advanced procedures, including initiating venous access, administering medications, performing endotracheal intubation, interpreting electrocardiograms (ECGs), delivering electrical cardiac therapy, performing chest decompression, establishing intraosseous access, and adhering to all state-defined Basic Life Support (BLS) protocols.
